To obtain the Joint Commission's Sustainable Healthcare Certification, a hospital must meet these requirements at the time of review [1][2]:

- Be in the United States, operated by the U.S. government, or operated under a charter of the U.S. Congress [1].
- Be a hospital or critical access hospital compliant with applicable federal laws, including applicable Medicare Conditions of Participation [1].
- Have baseline emissions data for three GHG emission sources and an action plan to reduce them [1].

For recertification, the organization needs 24 months of data and must demonstrate a reduction across three GHG emission sources [1].

**Emission sources it can choose to track** — organizations must collect data on 3 of the following [1]:

- Energy use (fuel combustion)
- Purchased electricity (purchased grid electricity, district steam, chilled and hot water)
- Anesthetic gas use, including volatile agents and nitrous oxide
- Pressurized metered-dose inhaler use
- Fleet vehicle carbon-based fuel use (from organization-owned vehicles)
- Waste disposal

Certified organizations convert their greenhouse gas measurements to metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalents (MTCO2e) [1].

# Scratch vs. pre-made: hospital and LTC operators

## Reasons for scratch cooking

**Long-term care** operators rank their top-3 benefits of scratch prep as: lower food costs (59%), better quality/tasting end product (49%), using the same ingredients across applications (38%), fresher dishes (38%), higher customer satisfaction (31%), less wastage (21%), healthier ingredients (16%), signature flavours (15%), more creative dishes (13%), more local ingredients (11%) and fewer availability issues (8%) [1].

**Hospital** operators give a similar but differently ordered set: better quality/tasting end product (57%), fresher dishes (43%), higher customer satisfaction (36%), lower food costs (35%), healthier ingredients (29%), less wastage (25%), more creative dishes (22%), same ingredients across applications (19%), signature flavours (13%), more local ingredients (10%) and fewer availability issues (9%) [8].

So both segments lead on quality/taste and freshness, but LTC puts cost first (59% vs 35%), while hospitals weight customer satisfaction and healthier ingredients somewhat higher [1][8].

## Reasons for pre-made products

**LTC** operators' top-3 benefits of fully-prepared products are: consistent quality/taste time after time (51%), less culinary skill required of staff (46%), able to serve items difficult to make (39%), staff has more time for other tasks (30%), easy to customise/"signaturise" (28%), less wastage (25%), better portion control (25%), less equipment/space needed (21%), lower costs (16%) and fewer products purchased (15%) [1].

**Hospital** operators cite: less culinary skill required of staff (49%), consistent quality/taste (48%), staff has more time for other tasks (42%), able to serve difficult-to-make items (34%), better portion control (31%), easy to customise (25%), fewer products purchased (18%), less equipment/space (17%), less wastage (14%) and lower costs (12%) [8].

The two segments largely agree, but hospitals rank **labour/skill relief first** (49%) and cost last (12%), whereas LTC ranks **consistency first** (51%) and also places cost low (16%) [1][8].

## How this relates to the Healthcare Segment Guide

The Guide says healthcare prep "tends to be more focused on scratch," because kitchens manage multiple specific diets (diabetic-friendly, low-sodium, etc.) and are less able to rely on prepared or semi-prepared items that may not meet nutritional or ingredient guidelines; in senior living, food is a key amenity, so operators want high quality and differentiation [2]. It also describes culinary skill as **moderate**: menus are generally simple and limited, so most hospital and LTC kitchens don't need high skill, while senior living tends to have more elaborate menus and possibly more skilled BOH staff [2]. Elsewhere the Guide lists "limited culinary skill" among operator pain points and "labor shortages/immigration reform" among key drivers [3]. For hospitals and LTC specifically, the focus is serving relatively healthful food to many patients/residents in a short window, so **ease of prep** and **holding well over long kitchen-to-room journeys** matter [2].

## What this implies for a supplier of sauces, bases and soups

- **The scratch orientation is real but qualified.** Operators say they cook from scratch mainly for quality, freshness and cost [1][8], and the Guide confirms a scratch-leaning prep style driven by diet specificity [2]. A supplier should therefore position products as *aids to scratch-style cooking* rather than replacements for it — e.g. bases and soups that let a kitchen build a low-sodium or diabetic-friendly item to spec, addressing the Guide's point that prepared items may not meet nutritional or ingredient guidelines [2].
- **Skill relief is the strongest single lever, especially in hospitals.** "Less culinary skill required of staff" is the top pre-made benefit for hospitals (49%) and second for LTC (46%) [1][8], and the Guide flags limited culinary skill as a pain point alongside labour shortages [3]. Bases and soups that deliver consistent results with minimal labour speak directly to this.
- **Consistency and holding performance matter.** Consistency is the top pre-made benefit in LTC (51%) and near-top in hospitals (48%) [1][8], and the Guide stresses that dishes must hold well on the journey from kitchen to patient room [2]. Soup and sauce formats with good hold times fit this need.
- **Cost is a weaker selling point than suppliers might assume.** Lower costs rank near the bottom of pre-made benefits in both segments (16% LTC, 12% hospital) [1][8], even though LTC names lower food costs as its top scratch benefit (59%) [1]. The pitch should lead on quality, consistency and labour, not price.
- **Diet and nutrition claims are a gate, not a bonus.** Because operators must work to specific diets under medical direction and there are local, state or federal patient-safety regulations [7], nutritional information/labelling is the most-used supplier service in LTC (75% using it, 52% via distributor) [9]. Clear nutritional documentation is effectively table stakes.
- **Support services are an opening.** LTC operators also want recipe ideas/menu suggestions (61%), product comparison tools (57%) and menu analysis/costing (49%) [9], and their most-desired insight is commodity prices (39%), followed by consumer trends (33%) and flavour trends (28%) [9]. A sauces/bases/soups supplier that bundles recipe and menu support with trend and price insight is addressing stated demand.
- **Route to market differs by operator type.** Large chains and national accounts purchase centrally through preferred/approved lists, often via contract feeders and GPOs, while independents and small chains buy decentrally, with dieticians and/or foodservice directors deciding [7]. Distribution is typically a mix of national broadline plus regional and local distributors in both cases [7].

**Bottom line:** the data support a positioning of sauces, bases and soups as consistency-and-labour solutions that still allow diet-compliant, scratch-style customisation — sold with strong nutritional documentation and menu/recipe support, and aimed at the dietician and foodservice director in decentralised accounts and at GPO/contract-feeder specifications in larger ones [2][3][7][9].

# Supplier Support Services and Information: PULSE 2026 vs. Selling Sustainability

## LTC operators (PULSE 2026)

**Supplier services used** — the most widely used services among LTC operators are nutritional information/labeling on products (75%), recipe ideas/menu suggestions (61%), product comparison tools (57%), menu analysis and costing (49%), and industry trend data (44%) [2]. Most of these are accessed via distributor rather than manufacturer [2].

**Desired insights** — LTC operators most want commodity prices (39%), consumer trends (33%), and flavor trends (28%) [2].

**Supplier attributes** — when choosing a supplier, LTC operators prioritise a good market reputation (59%), rigorous food safety measures (52%), exceptional quality standards (50%), and product guarantees (48%) [1].

**Year-over-year shifts** — LTC use of supplier services has risen sharply versus 2024, led by recipe ideas/menu suggestions (+28%), product comparison tools (+19%), and menu analysis and costing (+17%); demand for commodity price and flavor trend insights also rose (+10% each), while nutritional information/labeling and inventory management tools declined in importance (−15% each) [3].

## Hospital operators (PULSE 2026)

The Hospital chapter in the context covers operator motivators, behaviour, and challenges — sales sentiment, cost pressures, sourcing shifts, and objectives [5]. **It does not report supplier services used, desired insights, or supplier-selection attributes for hospitals.** So the context does not allow a like-for-like comparison of hospital support-service wants against LTC.

## Sustainability information needs (Selling Sustainability)

- Manufacturers can help operators improve sustainability efforts by providing **sustainable packaging and detailed ingredient listings including sources** [4].
- Operators mainly get sustainability information from **trade shows, peers, online sources, and distributors** [6].
- Operators are not fully exploiting advertising; the most effective channels to communicate sustainability programmes to consumers are **social media, the location's website, menu notes, and in-unit signage** [9].
- Cost is a constraint: most operators can pay only slightly more for sustainable items, so cost-effective, informative support — including noting sourcing and recycled/recyclable packaging on ingredient lists — helps them decide [9].

**Overlap:** both sources point to **detailed product/ingredient information and sourcing transparency** as a key supplier-provided need — nutritional labeling in PULSE [2] and ingredient sourcing plus packaging detail in Selling Sustainability [4]. **Divergence:** PULSE frames wants around operational and commercial support (menu costing, comparison tools, commodity price insight) [2][3], while Selling Sustainability frames them around sustainability communication and cost-effective sustainable options [4][9]. The context does not contain a regulation that *requires* hospital or LTC foodservice operators to meet sustainability standards. What it contains is a mix of voluntary certification, corporate pledges, and general regulatory frameworks that apply to organisations (not specifically to foodservice). Here is the breakdown by source.

## Voluntary certification (not regulation)

- **The Joint Commission – Sustainable Healthcare Certification** [1][3]: explicitly described as a **voluntary** certification that "any hospital or critical access hospital may apply for" [3]. It sets eligibility conditions — US-based or US-government/Congress-chartered, hospital or critical access hospital compliant with applicable federal laws including Medicare Conditions of Participation, baseline emissions data for three GHG sources plus a reduction action plan, and at recertification 24 months of data showing reduction of three GHG sources [1]. Certified organisations must collect data on 3 of six listed emissions types and convert them to MTCO2e [1]. This is a certification framework, not a legal requirement.

## Corporate pledges and targets (not regulation)

- **Sodexo – Better Tomorrow 2028** [8]: a company commitment, including an SBTi Net Zero target of 2040 and tracking of Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, plus the Stop Hunger philanthropic cause. This is a corporate pledge, not a regulation.

## Regulatory and standards frameworks (general, not foodservice-specific)

- **Mölnlycke consensus paper** [6][7]: notes increasing legal requirements to consider sustainability in procurement, and lists EU instruments — CSRD, CS3D, EU Taxonomy, EUDR, Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive, Whistleblowing Directive, Green Taxonomy, and planned ESPR and Digital Product Passport — plus national laws (German LkSG, Swiss conflict minerals/child labour directive, Norwegian Transparency Act, Belgian and Dutch proposals) [7]. It also mentions waste sorting/recycling obligations and the "polluter pays" principle [6][7]. These are framed as procurement and reporting obligations on organisations generally, not as standards that hospital or LTC foodservice operators must meet.
- **Practice Greenhealth** [9]: describes sustainable procurement as a voluntary practice aligned with "first do no harm" and the UN Sustainable Development Goals (Goal 12), not as a mandate.
- **Mölnlycke – supplier certifications and standards** [4][5][10]: SBTi, Responsibility Europe, PSCI, ISO 50001, ISO 45001, SA8000, EcoVadis, SEDEX, MSCI, SASB, Cradle to Cradle. These are third-party labels, platforms and standards used to assess suppliers — voluntary tools, not regulations.

## Foodservice-specific material

- **Datassential – Healthcare Segment Guide** [2]: describes purchasing structures (centralised for large chains/national accounts, decentralised for independents and small chains; contract feeders such as Aramark, Sodexo, Compass; GPOs such as Avendra, Entegra, Foodbuy, Premier) and notes that "there are rarely specific nutritional guidelines," though local, state or federal regulations may exist for patient safety, with diets under medical direction [2]. It does **not** mention any sustainability standard or requirement for foodservice operators.

**Bottom line:** the only sustainability-specific scheme in the corpus aimed at hospitals is a voluntary certification [1][3]; the Sodexo item is a corporate pledge [8]; the EU and national instruments are general legal/reporting frameworks [6][7]; and the foodservice passages describe purchasing structures and patient-safety regulation, not sustainability mandates [2].

# Section 3 — Segment patrons: Hospital foodservice

## Who hospital foodservice patrons are

Healthcare foodservice covers patient feeding, employee feeding, visitor meals and catering at institutions such as hospitals, long-term care facilities and senior living communities [7]. Within hospitals specifically, offerings tend to be in-room feeding for patients plus cafeterias for employees and visitors, and some locations have QSRs, fast-casual restaurants, coffee shops or sit-down restaurants [7]. Dining services for hospitals almost always include patient feeding but can also include staff and visitor options such as a cafeteria, restaurants and retail/snack shops [5]. Visitors and employees are most likely to have a limited-service experience — usually cafeteria-style, where they select items, carry food to their table and bus their own tables — though some hospitals are adding partial- or full-service options with waitstaff [7]. Patient food costs are generally baked into the cost of the overall stay, so they are seen as both "free" and very costly [7].

So the hospital patron set is threefold: **patients/residents** (in-room, ordered ahead or increasingly on-demand), **employees**, and **visitors** [7].

## U.S. Plastics Pact targets

The Pact aims for an average of 30% postconsumer recycled content (PCR) by weight, or responsibly-sourced biobased content, across the U.S. packaging portfolio. It prioritizes PCR in packaging with the fewest challenges (e.g., rigid plastic packaging) while adhering to food safety requirements, and works toward PCR mandates to create market demand. This aligns with Target 2's goal of 100% reusability, recyclability, or compostability by 2025 [8].

Responsibly-sourced biobased content must meet five WWF-US criteria and have proven credible certification: legally sourced and conforming to the UDHR with safe/healthy production; derived from renewable biomass; not adversely impacting food security and affordability; not destroying critical ecosystems or High Conservation Value habitats; and contributing to landscape resilience and climate resilience [8]. The Pact also notes that biobased content addresses feedstock sources (not end-of-life characteristics like compostability or biodegradability) and permits plastic derived from plants or other biomass [3].

On reuse definitions, the Pact specifies that packaging is reusable if its design enables principal components to accomplish multiple trips or rotations under normally predictable conditions (ISO 18603), and that a "system for reuse" must be in place with a provable significant actual reuse rate. Single-use packaging delivering a refill for a reusable package is not considered reusable [2][9].

Premier Inc. reports that its EPP (Environmentally Preferable Purchasing) Advisory Council advises on EPP matters for contracts and serves as a forum for members to drive sustainability in healthcare. Recent discussions have focused on plastic elimination in the foodservice setting, composting and waste disposal, and contractual barriers to increased reuse and reprocessing [5].

## Where a foodservice supplier's packaging would be judged

Based on the context, a supplier's packaging would be assessed against the U.S. Plastics Pact's criteria: the 30% PCR/biobased content target and the 100% reusability, recyclability, or compostability goal by 2025 [8], along with the Pact's definitions of reusable packaging and "systems for reuse" [2][9], and the five WWF-US criteria plus credible certification for responsibly-sourced biobased content [8].
